questions.question: An 82-year-old with stable mild dementia becomes sleepy, inattentive, and intermittently disoriented over two days after starting an over-the-counter sleep aid. What is the best initial interpretation?
choices: Expected progression of dementia
Hypoactive delirium with a possible medication contributor
Normal aging
A permanent loss of decision-making capacity
questions.explanation: Acute onset, fluctuation, and impaired attention point to delirium. Hypoactive delirium is easily missed, and sedating or anticholinergic products may contribute; urgent assessment for additional medical causes is still required.

questions.question: Which set correctly identifies the Geriatrics 5Ms?
choices: Memory, Metabolism, Muscle, Money, Mortality
Mind, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, Matters Most
Monitoring, Meals, Mood, Movement, Medicine
Mentation, Malignancy, Microbiology, Morphology, Management
questions.explanation: The 5Ms are Mind, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, and Matters Most. They provide an integrated framework rather than five isolated checkboxes.

questions.question: A 79-year-old taking an anticoagulant falls, has a scalp bruise and new headache, and cannot recall whether consciousness was lost. What is the safest next step?
choices: Label the event a mechanical fall and review next month
Stop the anticoagulant permanently without assessment
Arrange urgent evaluation for head injury and the cause of possible syncope
Recommend only a home grab bar
questions.explanation: Head impact, anticoagulation, headache, and possible loss of consciousness create an urgent risk for intracranial injury and a potentially serious cause of syncope. Fall prevention can follow after immediate threats are addressed.

questions.question: Which statement best describes appropriate use of the AGS Beers Criteria?
choices: Every listed medication must be stopped immediately
The criteria replace medication reconciliation
They identify potentially inappropriate patterns that require individualized benefit-harm review
Any medication not listed is safe in every older adult
questions.explanation: Beers Criteria support identification of medication risk but do not replace judgment. Indication, alternatives, kidney function, interactions, withdrawal risk, goals, and monitoring determine the patient-specific plan.

questions.question: A frail 88-year-old with low muscle mass becomes excessively sedated after the dose of a renally cleared drug is increased. Serum creatinine is within the reference range. What should the FNP recognize?
choices: Normal creatinine excludes medication accumulation
Low muscle mass may mask impaired kidney filtration
The medication cannot cause sedation
Renal function has no role in geriatric prescribing
questions.explanation: Creatinine generation falls with low muscle mass, so a seemingly normal serum level can coexist with reduced filtration. Reassess the renal estimate, medication dose, hydration, interactions, and other causes.

questions.question: An older adult with mild cognitive impairment refuses a procedure but can explain the condition, options, personal consequences, and a consistent reason for refusal. Which is the best conclusion?
choices: Cognitive impairment automatically removes capacity
Refusal itself proves incapacity
Capacity should be assessed for this decision, and the described abilities support honoring the choice
Only a family member may decide after age 75
questions.explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and includes communicating a choice, understanding, appreciation, and reasoning. A cognitive diagnosis or disagreement with clinicians does not independently establish incapacity.

questions.question: Which intervention has a USPSTF grade B recommendation for community-dwelling adults age 65 or older who are at increased risk for falls?
choices: Routine bed rest
Exercise interventions
Automatic discontinuation of all antihypertensives
Vitamin supplementation as the only assessment
questions.explanation: USPSTF recommends exercise interventions for older community-dwelling adults at increased fall risk. Care should also assess modifiable risks such as medications, gait, orthostasis, vision, feet, and environment.

questions.question: An 86-year-old with frailty, recurrent falls, CKD, diabetes, and symptomatic orthostasis takes 14 medications. What is the best next step?
choices: Intensify every disease target simultaneously
Stop every medication on the same day
Clarify goals, reconcile the actual regimen, prioritize harms and benefits, and create a monitored plan
Ignore orthostasis because hypertension carries long-term risk
questions.explanation: Multimorbidity creates competing recommendations. Goal-concordant care prioritizes immediate threats, function, treatment burden, time-to-benefit, and medication safety with monitored changes.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly suggests delirium rather than uncomplicated early dementia?
choices: Gradual memory decline over several years
Acute fluctuation with impaired attention
Stable difficulty balancing a checkbook
A family history of Alzheimer disease
questions.explanation: Delirium is characterized by acute or subacute change, fluctuation, inattention, and altered awareness. It requires evaluation for medical, toxic, medication, environmental, and withdrawal causes.

questions.question: Which discharge plan best closes the loop after hospitalization of a frail older adult?
choices: Copy the discharge medication list without comparison
Assume the specialist owns every pending result
Reconcile actual medications, assess new functional needs and caregiver capacity, assign pending-result ownership, and arrange early follow-up
Delay contact until the next annual visit
questions.explanation: Transitions create medication, function, equipment, and follow-up hazards. Safe closure requires comparison of medication lists, feasibility assessment, explicit ownership of pending items, and timely reassessment.
